candidate.title: Random-matrix prediction becomes inspectable through finite products

parents.title: Characteristic-polynomial limits supply the previously mysterious universal constants

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: For each symmetry type X in {U, O, Sp}, a characteristic-polynomial limit gives a gamma-product candidate for g_{lambda,X}. Keeping Gamma(1+B_X(lambda)) visible is not cosmetic: absorbing it would hide the arithmetic origins of the moment parameters and the integrality of g_k at positive integers, whereas the quotient g_lambda/Gamma(1+B(lambda)) is precisely the nonvanishing meromorphic function of order two whose poles the paper describes. This normalization therefore separates an analytic object from arithmetic structure; agreement at small k calibrates, but does not prove, the conjectural transfer to L-function moments.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: The reading compares the two normalization choices and assigns distinct mathematical work to their factors: the quotient carries the stated analytic continuation and pole structure, while the displayed Gamma normalization retains visible arithmetic information. The alternative normalization gains compactness but loses that visibility, leaving the conjectural random-matrix-to-L-function bridge as the outstanding proof burden.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: Accepted after restoring the critic-required quotient g_lambda/Gamma(1+B(lambda)) as the exact order-two meromorphic object and preserving the conjectural-transfer boundary; the relevant formulas are legible in the assigned span.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: Equations (2.1)-(2.3) state the U, O, and Sp limits with their respective B_X(lambda), and the text says they agree with known and conjectural g_k values. It then states both that g_lambda/Gamma(1+B(lambda)) is nonvanishing meromorphic of order two with completely described pole locations and that g_k is integral for positive integer k.
accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: The meromorphic-quotient and positive-integer integrality claims are reported source results. The identification of the normalization as an analytic/arithmetic interface is an interpretation of those results. The L-function moment transfer remains conjectural, and low-k agreement is only calibration.

parents.title: Second differences of log Gamma control an infinite product as an order-two meromorphic function

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: Finite differencing exposes precisely the common growth canceled by the normalization.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: Second log-Gamma differences, the derivative estimate, normalization, and pole sequence bridge the product to meromorphic growth.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: Source fact: the unitary gamma-product tail becomes a second finite difference of log Gamma, a derivative estimate gives 1/j plus a summable error, subtraction of lambda^2 log N yields convergence and order at most two, and pole exponent of convergence supplies exact order two. None identified; the output limits the detailed proof to U and does not claim it proves any L-function moment. The cancellation language is directly supported by the finite-difference calculation and normalization.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: For the unitary case, log Gamma(j)-2log Gamma(j+lambda)+log Gamma(j+2lambda) equals lambda^2 f_j''(xi). An integral formula gives f_j''(xi)=1/j+O((xi+1)/j^2), proving convergence after subtracting lambda^2 log N and order at most two. The poles have exponent of convergence two.
accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: The unit illustrates U and declares other cases similar; it does not prove L-function moments. The extraction is sufficient and legible. Reasonable inference: finite differencing isolates the common growth removed by normalization. The extraction is legible and no formula reconstruction is needed.

parents.selection_reason: Regrouped factorial products yield exact p-adic floor sums; decomposing each summand into two residue cases makes it an integer strictly greater than -1, hence nonnegative.
parents.title: Floor-sum decompositions prove every p-adic valuation is nonnegative

accepted_interpretation.interpretation: Regrouping factorial and odd-double-factorial products converts the global integrality question into p-adic floor sums indexed by valuation layer ell. For every odd prime p, the orthogonal summand and each of the two exhaustive unitary residue cases are rewritten as integers strictly greater than -1, hence as nonnegative contributions; their sums give nonnegative odd-prime valuations. This representation gains a prime-by-prime, scale-by-scale certificate and exposes residue geometry hidden by the gamma-product form, but it depends on the exact floor conventions and does not itself supply the omitted p=2 argument.
accepted_interpretation.nonparaphrase_operation: The reading decomposes integrality into local certificates along two axes, prime p and layer ell, and explains why the two unitary residue cases are the exhaustive obstruction check. This exposes where nonnegativity is proved and what the representation costs: specialized floor notation must be preserved exactly, and the detailed proof burden for p=2 lies outside the displayed layerwise argument.
accepted_interpretation.quality_reason: Accepted after correcting the boundary to distinguish the detailed odd-prime proof from the span's unsupported-by-detail p=2 assertion; exact floor conventions and both unitary residue cases are retained.
accepted_interpretation.source_support: Lemma 5.3 gives the factorial and odd-double-factorial valuation formulas, including the special convention [x]_2=[([x]+1)/2]. Proposition 5.4 supplies exact floor sums. Equations (5.1)-(5.3) show the orthogonal layer and the two unitary cases are greater than -1 and integral, so each is nonnegative. The span explicitly assumes p>2 and only says divisibility by a large power of 2 is easy.
accepted_interpretation.speculation_status: The odd-prime layerwise nonnegativity and residue-case split are proved in the assigned span. The prime p=2 is merely set aside there as easy, not established by the displayed derivation. The residue-geometry description is a supported conceptual interpretation, not an additional theorem.
